intro_en: In this lesson you will learn to point at things that are near, a little far, and far away, and to ask and answer "What is this?" and "Whose is that?". Just as Tamil has the demonstratives "இது / அது" (this / that) and "இந்த / அந்த" (this … / that …), Japanese has これ・それ・あれ and この・その・あの. The difference is that Japanese has three distance levels. The lesson also covers words for stationery, everyday objects and names of languages.

g02-1.explanation_en: There are three words for pointing at things: これ = something near the speaker ("this", இது), それ = something near the listener ("that", அது), あれ = something far from both ("that over there", அதோ அது). Modern Tamil commonly uses only two, "இது / அது"; but Old Tamil and Sri Lankan Tamil have a middle demonstrative "உது", and that is exactly それ. These words behave like nouns, so they take particles such as は, も and の directly: これは、それも. If I ask 「これは 何ですか」, the listener answers 「それは ペンです」, because what is near me is a little far from them.
g02-1.tamil_parallel_en: இது புத்தகம் "This is a book" / அது பேனா "That is a pen" / அதோ அது கடிகாரம் "That over there is a clock" = これは 本です。/ それは ペンです。/ あれは 時計です。 Tamil "இது / அது" map to これ / それ・あれ, with Japanese adding a third distance.
g02-1.formation_en: これ / それ / あれ + は + N + です
g02-1.pitfalls_en: Because Tamil "அது" (that) covers both それ and あれ, remember: if it is near the listener, use それ; if it is far from both of you, use あれ. A noun cannot come directly after これ・それ・あれ (「これ本」 is wrong).

g02-2.explanation_en: これ・それ・あれ stand alone as "this / that"; but to say "this book, that pen" together with a noun, you use この・その・あの. Just as Tamil changes "இது" (this) → "இந்த" (this …) and "அது" (that) → "அந்த" (that …), Japanese changes これ → この, それ → その, あれ → あの. The distance rule is the same as before: この = near me, その = near you, あの = far from both of us. A noun must come after この・その・あの; they never stand alone, just as in Tamil you don't stop after saying only "இந்த" (this …).
g02-2.tamil_parallel_en: இந்தப் புத்தகம் என்னுடையது "This book is mine" = この本は 私のです。 Here この is roughly "இந்த" (this …), and その / あの are roughly "அந்த" (that …).
g02-2.formation_en: この / その / あの + N + は …
g02-2.pitfalls_en: Putting は right after この, as in 「このは 本です」, is wrong; a noun must follow この. "This is a book" = これは 本です, "this book" = この本; don't mix the two up.

g02-3.explanation_en: In the last lesson, の showed which organisation someone belongs to; in this lesson it has two more jobs. First, possession: 「私の 本」 = my book (என் புத்தகம்), 「田中さんの 傘」 = Tanaka-san's umbrella (தனாகா-சானின் குடை), exactly like the Tamil "-இன் / -உடைய" (of / 's). Second, content or type: 「日本語の 本」 = a Japanese-language book (ஜப்பானிய மொழிப் புத்தகம்), 「英語の 字引」 = an English dictionary (ஆங்கில அகராதி). In Tamil we just put the words side by side here with no ending, but in Japanese の is required. The owner / type always comes first and the thing comes after, the same order as Tamil.
g02-3.tamil_parallel_en: என் புத்தகம் "my book" / ஜப்பானிய மொழிப் புத்தகம் "Japanese-language book" = 私の 本 / 日本語の 本. Here の is roughly the Tamil "-இன் / -உடைய" (of / 's), or a type link where Tamil simply puts the two words side by side.
g02-3.pitfalls_en: Don't write "Japanese book" as 「日本語本」 without の. "My" = 私の; using は, as in 「私は 本」, is wrong.

g02-4.explanation_en: To answer a 「〜は N ですか」 question briefly without repeating the whole noun, you use そう: 「はい、そうです」 = "Yes, that's right / it is" (ஆமாம், அப்படித்தான் / அதுதான்), 「いいえ、そうじゃありません」 = "No, it isn't" (இல்லை, அப்படி இல்லை). It is just like answering the Tamil "இது பேனாவா?" (Is this a pen?) with "ஆமாம், அதுதான்" (yes, that's it). For a negative answer, people also say 「いいえ、違います」 instead of そうじゃありません. Note: そうです is only for questions about nouns; questions with verbs and adjectives come later. 「そうですか」 said with a falling voice means "I see" (அப்படியா), showing you have understood.
g02-4.tamil_parallel_en: "இது பேனாவா?" "Is this a pen?" — "ஆமாம், அதுதான்." "Yes, it is." / "இல்லை, அப்படி இல்லை." "No, it isn't." = 「これは ペンですか。」「はい、そうです。」/「いいえ、そうじゃありません。」 Like Tamil "அதுதான் / அப்படி இல்லை", そう stands in for the noun.
g02-4.formation_en: はい、そうです / いいえ、そうじゃありません (= いいえ、違います)
g02-4.pitfalls_en: You can't answer a 何 question such as "What is this?" with そうです; there you must say the noun. Don't combine はい with a denial, as in 「はい、そうじゃありません」.

g02-5.explanation_en: To ask "which of the two?", just put the two questions one after the other: 「これは ペンですか、鉛筆ですか」. Just as Tamil adds "-ஆ" to both in "இது பேனாவா, பென்சிலா?" (Is this a pen or a pencil?), Japanese puts ですか after both; you don't need a word for "or". You must not answer this question with はい / いいえ; you say the one you choose: 「ペンです」. In Tamil too, if someone asks "பேனாவா பென்சிலா?" (pen or pencil?), we don't answer "ஆமாம்" (yes), do we?
g02-5.tamil_parallel_en: இது பேனாவா, பென்சிலா? — பேனா. "Is this a pen or a pencil? — A pen." = これは ペンですか、鉛筆ですか。— ペンです。 Like the Tamil "-ஆ" on both choices, ですか goes on both.
g02-5.formation_en: N1 は A ですか、B ですか。 → A です / B です
g02-5.pitfalls_en: Don't forget ですか on the second part too (「ペンですか、鉛筆」 is wrong). The answer is not 「はい」; say which of the two it is.

g02-6.explanation_en: "What is this?" = 「これは 何ですか」 (なん). "Whose is this?" = 「これは 誰のですか」. Here the noun after 誰の (本, かばん) has been dropped; の itself carries the meaning "belonging to". It is just like shortening Tamil "என் புத்தகம்" (my book) → "என்னுடையது" (mine), and "ராஜாவின் பை" (Raja's bag) → "ராஜாவுடையது" (Raja's). So 「私のです」 = "It's mine" (என்னுடையது), 「田中さんのです」 = "It's Tanaka-san's" (தனாகா-சானுடையது). Question words (何, 誰) stay in the middle of the sentence, before です, just as in Tamil; don't move them to the front as in English.
g02-6.tamil_parallel_en: இது யாருடையது? — என்னுடையது. "Whose is this? — It's mine." = これは 誰のですか。— 私のです。 Here の is roughly the Tamil "-உடையது" (the one belonging to).
g02-6.formation_en: N は 何ですか ; N は 誰のですか → (person) のです
g02-6.pitfalls_en: 「誰ですか」 = "Who?" (யார்?), 「誰のですか」 = "Whose?" (யாருடையது?); if you drop の, the meaning changes. Before です, 何 is read なん (not なに).

g02-7.explanation_en: Adding お before certain nouns that belong to someone else makes them polite: お名前 = your name (உங்கள் பெயர்), お国 = your country (உங்கள் நாடு). It is like adding "தங்கள்" (your, respectful) in Tamil: "பெயர்" (name) → "தங்கள் பெயர்", "ஊர்" (hometown) → "தங்கள் ஊர்". Important rule: never add お when talking about yourself: 「私の 名前は ラジャです」 (私の お名前 is wrong). You can't add お to every word; only to some familiar ones (お名前、お国、おいくつ). Katakana words (カメラ, ペン) don't take お.
g02-7.tamil_parallel_en: தங்கள் பெயர்? "Your name?" / தங்கள் நாடு? "Your country?" = お名前は？ / お国は？ Here お works like the respectful Tamil "தங்கள்" (your).
g02-7.formation_en: お + N (someone else's) ; no お for your own
g02-7.pitfalls_en: 「私の お名前」: adding お to your own thing is wrong. お is not a separate word; write it joined to the noun (おなまえ).

items.L02-q01: 時計 = とけい (கடிகாரம், clock / watch). It ends with the long sound けい; shortening it to とけ or changing the sound to どけい is wrong.
items.L02-q02: 英語 = えいご (ஆங்கிலம், English). 語 is ご (not こ); don't shorten the long sound えい to えご.
items.L02-q03: 鉛筆 = えんぴつ (பென்சில், pencil). 筆 alone is ひつ, but after 鉛 it changes to ぴつ; えんひつ / えんびつ are wrong.
items.L02-q04: かさ = 傘 (குடை, umbrella). 金, 全 and 命 are look-alike characters that all have a 人 shape on top; 傘 has four small 人 inside.
items.L02-q05: ほん = 本 (புத்தகம், book). Add a short stroke at the bottom of 木 (மரம், tree) and you get 本; 体 and 休 are different characters that contain 木.
items.L02-q06: The answer uses それ (the thing near you), so the question uses これ (the thing near me). この / その / あの need a noun after them; は cannot come directly after them.
items.L02-q07: The answer is "mine", so the question is "whose" = 誰の (யாருடைய). If it were なん (என்ன, what), the answer would be an object.
items.L02-q08: カメラ (camera) is a word written in katakana. In hiragana it would be かめら.
items.L02-q09: The thing that can be "… of the Japanese language" is a dictionary (字引, அகராதி). A key, an umbrella and a clock don't have a language.
items.L02-q10: For a noun question like "Is it a pen?", "Yes, it is" = はい、そうです. あれ is the demonstrative "that over there" (அதோ அது) and doesn't fit here.
items.L02-q11: What can come before the noun 人 is あの (அந்த, that …). あれ / それ / これ are demonstratives that stand alone; they don't come before a noun.
items.L02-q12: "This book is mine" = "This is my book" (இது என் புத்தகம்). 本 has been dropped after 私の; the first option is a negative.
items.L02-q13: そうじゃありません = "it isn't" (அப்படி இல்லை), that is, "that is not a pencil" (பென்சில் இல்லை). "That is a pencil too" (も) is the opposite.
items.L02-q14: 山田さんの = "Yamada-san's" (யமாடா-சானுடையது); the dropped noun is 時計 (clock). "Yamada-san is a clock" is a meaningless sentence.
items.L02-q15: The demonstrative noun これ is the topic, so は. If you put の, the meaning changes to "this one's bag" and the sentence doesn't finish.
items.L02-q16: Before the noun 本, use この (இந்த, this …). これ (இது, this) only stands alone; 「これ本」 is wrong.
items.L02-q17: "English dictionary" (ஆங்கில அகராதி) uses the type-linking の. は does not appear twice in one sentence.
items.L02-q18: If the asker says それ (near you), then for the person answering it is これ (near me). Distance changes depending on who is speaking.
items.L02-q19: "Is it Tanaka-san's?" (தனாகா-சானுடையதா?) = 田中さんのですか; の gives the meaning "belonging to". Using は would put two は in one sentence.
items.L02-q20: In an "A or B?" question, か is required on the second part too. Using も gives a different meaning, "a pencil too".
items.L02-q21: It starts with いいえ, so it is a denial: 私のじゃありません = "It's not mine" (என்னுடையது இல்லை). Using です would contradict いいえ.
items.L02-q22: これは 私の 日本語の 本です。 — owner (私の) → type (日本語の) → thing (本). 日本語の goes in the ★ slot.
items.L02-q23: そのかばんは 誰のですか。 — その comes before the noun, and 誰の before です. 誰の goes in the ★ slot.
items.L02-q24: あれは ペンですか、鉛筆ですか。 — both choices take ですか; 鉛筆 goes in the ★ slot.
items.L02-q25: ［1］ "Japanese-language teacher" (ஜப்பானிய மொழி ஆசிரியர்) uses the type-linking の. ［2］ "Not the teacher's, it's mine" = 私のです; here の means "belonging to". ［3］ The second か of an "A or B?" question.
